topic: How Spring resolves constructor dependencies with multiple bean candidates
tomorrowTopic: Diagnosing unexpected React effect reruns from unstable dependencies

hook.headline: Spring does not guess between matching beans
hook.hook: Constructor injection starts with candidate beans matching the dependency type, then uses narrowing rules when more than one candidate exists.
hook.visualCaption: A single-valued dependency needs one resolvable candidate after Spring applies its autowiring selection rules.
hook.microExample: two PaymentClient beans → qualifier narrows → one injected

mentalModel.title: Resolve, then inject
mentalModel.coreIdea: For a single constructor parameter, Spring first finds autowire candidates compatible with the required type. If several remain, metadata such as qualifiers or a primary candidate can narrow the choice; unresolved ambiguity causes bean creation to fail rather than selecting arbitrarily.
mentalModel.keyOutcome: Constructor injection makes dependency ambiguity visible during container creation instead of hiding an arbitrary selection.

code.title: Qualify the injection point
code.intro: Use a qualifier when the dependency requires a specific implementation among multiple beans of one type.
code.highlightReason: The qualifier narrows compatible PaymentClient candidates to those carrying the matching qualifier metadata.
code.takeaway: The declared type defines the candidate set; qualification expresses which candidate this dependency intends to use.
code.professionalNote: Prefer explicit qualification when multiple implementations have distinct business roles instead of relying on incidental bean naming.

production.title: When a second implementation breaks startup
production.scenario: A team adds a second PaymentClient implementation for a migration. CheckoutService previously had one type match, but now its unqualified constructor parameter has multiple eligible candidates.
problems: The dependency becomes ambiguous and application-context creation can fail.
Marking one implementation primary may hide whether every consumer actually intends that default.
production.professionalApproach: Decide whether one implementation is genuinely the application-wide default. Use a primary candidate for that case; otherwise qualify consumers so each dependency communicates its intended implementation.
production.debugClue: Startup reports that a single dependency expected one bean but multiple candidates of the required type are available.

interview.question: How does Spring decide what to inject when a constructor parameter has multiple beans of the same interface type?
interview.answer: Spring resolves autowiring candidates compatible with the parameter type, then applies candidate-selection metadata such as qualifiers or a primary designation. If a single-valued dependency still has multiple eligible candidates, Spring does not choose one arbitrarily; bean creation fails. I use qualifiers when implementations represent distinct roles and primary only for a genuine default.
